cards.title: Breakthrough science often advances by ignoring the scientific method
cards.body: Philosophers long searched for a single, universal method that separates science from pseudoscience. In 1975, Paul Feyerabend shattered that ambition in Against Method. Examining historical breakthroughs like Galileo's defense of heliocentrism, Feyerabend showed that pioneers routinely ignored data, broke rules of formal logic, and relied on propaganda to persuade peers. Science thrives on opportunistic freedom, leading Feyerabend to argue that the only universal principle that survives scrutiny is: "anything goes."

cards.title: An ancient Roman poet used an atomic glitch to save free will
cards.body: Over two millennia before quantum mechanics, the Roman poet Lucretius faced a chilling philosophical dilemma. If the universe consists entirely of material atoms falling endlessly through empty space under deterministic physical laws, how could matter collide to form worlds—and how could humans possess free will? Lucretius proposed the clinamen, or "swerve": at completely unpredictable times and places, atoms veer ever so slightly off course, breaking the deterministic chain and creating room for genuine human agency.

cards.title: Why a political leader can do the right thing and still be morally guilty
cards.body: Can an action be politically necessary yet morally wrong? In 1973, philosopher Michael Walzer explored the "problem of dirty hands." Leaders often face emergencies where safeguarding their citizens requires authorizing heinous acts, such as torture to stop a ticking bomb. While utilitarian calculations might declare the act justified, Walzer argued the leader does not escape guilt. A conscientious leader must acknowledge that their moral hands are genuinely dirty, bearing the heavy cost of a violated rule.

cards.title: You cannot understand someone without assuming they are mostly right
cards.body: How do you interpret someone speaking an unknown language? Philosopher Donald Davidson argued that communication relies on the "principle of charity." To make sense of another person's words, you must start from the premise that most of their beliefs about the world are rational and true. Translation cannot even begin by treating a speaker as thoroughly mistaken, because identifying someone's specific errors requires an immense background of shared, accurate beliefs about reality.

cards.title: Why the universe's fine-tuning shouldn't surprise us at all
cards.body: Many fundamental physical constants seem miraculously fine-tuned for life. If gravity were slightly stronger or electromagnetism weaker, stars would fail to form and life could not emerge. In 1973, physicist Brandon Carter formulated the Anthropic Principle to address this puzzle. He argued that what observers witness is constrained by the conditions necessary for their existence. We should never be surprised to find ourselves in a life-permitting universe, because in a hostile one, nobody exists to ask.

quizzes.question: According to philosopher Paul Feyerabend, which rule governs all successful scientific breakthroughs?
options: Falsify every hypothesis rigorously
"Anything goes"
Always choose the simplest explanation
Rely strictly on inductive logic
quizzes.explanation: In Against Method, Feyerabend argued that historical breakthroughs routinely violated fixed rules of logic and evidence, leaving "anything goes" as the only universal maxim.

quizzes.question: What did the Roman poet Lucretius propose to explain how free will can exist in a mechanistic, atomic universe?
options: The clinamen, a minute and unpredictable atomic swerve
Direct intervention by Olympian gods in human minds
An immaterial soul completely immune to physical forces
A mystical balance between fire and water elements
quizzes.explanation: Lucretius introduced the clinamen—an unpredictable, random swerve in falling atoms—to break rigid causal chains and allow for free will and cosmic collisions.

quizzes.question: What is the core premise of Michael Walzer's "problem of dirty hands" in political ethics?
options: Political leaders who commit necessary wrongs remain morally guilty
Any action that saves a nation is automatically morally pure
Moral considerations have zero legitimate place in governance
Utilitarian math completely erases the wrongdoing of any act
quizzes.explanation: Walzer argued that even when committing an abhorrent act is politically necessary to prevent catastrophe, the leader does not become innocent; their hands remain dirty.

quizzes.question: What does Donald Davidson's "principle of charity" require when interpreting another person's speech?
options: Assuming that most of their beliefs are rational and true
Forgiving any insults or logical fallacies they express
Translating their sentences into symbolic mathematical logic
Assuming they are confused until they cite hard evidence
quizzes.explanation: Davidson argued that translation is impossible unless we start with the presumption that the speaker is rational and that most of their beliefs about reality are accurate.

quizzes.question: How does the Anthropic Principle explain why our universe's physical constants permit life?
options: Observers can only ever witness conditions compatible with their existence
Cosmic evolution guarantees that all universes eventually produce minds
The laws of physics dynamically adjust whenever living beings observe them
Gravity and electromagnetism are mathematically required to be equal
quizzes.explanation: The Anthropic Principle points out an observation selection effect: we could never find ourselves in a universe whose fundamental laws prevent observers from emerging.

misconceptions.claim: Major scientific revolutions have strictly followed the formal scientific method.
misconceptions.explanation: Paul Feyerabend demonstrated that historical pioneers like Galileo routinely ignored data and broke formal rules of logic to advance revolutionary theories.

misconceptions.claim: Ancient Roman philosophers theorized that random atomic glitches explain human free will.
misconceptions.explanation: Over 2,000 years ago, Lucretius posited the clinamen—an unpredictable, random swerve of falling atoms—to explain free agency within physical nature.

misconceptions.claim: The universe's fine-tuning proves it was purposefully designed to produce human beings.
misconceptions.explanation: The Anthropic Principle shows that observers will inevitably find themselves in a life-permitting universe, because in a hostile one, nobody exists to make observations.
